WHO IS WILLIAM F. MOHRMAN? William F. Mohrman is a longtime Minneapolis lawyer and former partner at the firm Mohrman, Kaardal & Erickson. He gained national attention as the attorney for Derek Chauvin following Chauvin’s conviction for murdering George Floyd, arguing that extensive pretrial publicity and security concerns deprived Chauvin of a fair trial and seeking to overturn the conviction on appeal. Courts rejected those arguments. ￼ HIS NEW ROLE AT DOJ Mohrman entered his first appearance on behalf of the United States in the DOJ’s lawsuit seeking Georgia’s unredacted statewide voter registration records. Court filings identify him as a senior counsel in the Civil Rights Division’s Voting Section, making him the latest in a growing list of attorneys added to the section who have worked on 2020 election challenges or teamed up with prominent election deniers. ￼ HIS 2020 ELECTION RECORD In the period after the 2020 election, Mohrman worked on cases aimed at blocking certification of Biden’s wins in Arizona and Georgia, as well as in the U.S. Congress. Court records show he was listed as counsel in litigation brought by the Wisconsin Voters Alliance, including a lawsuit that sought to block congressional certification of Biden’s Electoral College victory shortly before January 6, 2021. U.S. District Judge James Boasberg dismissed the case, describing the claims as meritless. ￼ THE BROADER VOTER DATA CAMPAIGN Two executive orders underpin the effort. Executive Order 14,248, signed in March 2025, directed the AG to pursue information-sharing agreements with state election officials and prioritize enforcement against non-cooperating states. Executive Order 14,399, signed in March 2026, directed the Secretary of Homeland Security to compile a list of confirmed U.S. citizens eligible to vote in each state from federal naturalization records, Social Security data, and the DHS SAVE immigration verification system. ￼ During a hearing in DOJ’s lawsuit seeking Rhode Island’s voter data, a DOJ attorney confirmed the information would be shared with Homeland Security. ￼ The strategy has unfolded on three fronts: cooperation from Republican-led states willing to share voter data, lawsuits against roughly two dozen blue and purple states that have refused, and a legislative push in Congress to tighten national voting requirements. Federal judges have so far rebuffed the Justice Department’s legal demands, but the Trump administration has continued widening its campaign ahead of the 2026 midterms. ￼ THE PUSHBACK Common Cause and four of its members sued the DOJ in April 2026 to block the creation of a national voter database and prevent voter data from being run through the SAVE program, which they argue could result in the purging of eligible voters. ￼ Democratic election officials, and some Republicans, have condemned the demands as an invasion of voter privacy, voicing concerns the Trump administration plans to use the information to target political opponents or create a national voter list. ￼ VERDICT: CONFIRMED — Tier 1 sourced. Primary source: Democracy Docket (June 4, 2026), based on court filings. Corroborated by Brennan Center tracker, Stateline, JURIST, and the University of Wisconsin Law School’s State Democracy Research Initiative. The core claim holds up under scrutiny. Mohrman’s hiring represents a documented pattern — the Civil Rights Division’s Voting Section has simultaneously shifted away from its traditional voting rights enforcement priorities and toward lawsuits seeking sensitive voter records from states and counties around the country. ￼
